1373.title: Traditional Sufi orders today
1373.hook: orders active from Senegal to Indonesia, like the Tijaniyyah and Muridiyyah
1373.howItsDone: Members of a Sufi order take a pledge with a shaykh, keep a daily wird of recitations such as asking forgiveness and blessings on the Prophet, and gather regularly for group dhikr; orders like the Tijaniyyah and Muridiyyah are active in West Africa, and others across Asia and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salafi approach: the Qur'an and Sunnah as the first generations understood them, by one road back.

Before dawn, in a courtyard, a circle of men sits on mats, prayer beads moving through their fingers. Across a wall, women sit in their own circle. Somebody begins a phrase, and the others take it up, again and again, low and steady, until the words feel less like speech and more like breathing. Nobody is performing. This is a morning, not a festival. Scenes like this happen in towns from Senegal to Indonesia, inside communities with names, teachers and daily rules of their own. These are the Sufi orders, and they are not a museum piece.
screen: `A CIRCLE BEFORE DAWN.` → `ONE PHRASE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `A LIVING ORDER, NOT A MUSEUM.`

segments.voice: An order is called a tariqa, a path. A person joins by taking a pledge with a living teacher, a shaykh, who in the order's understanding stands in a chain of teachers reaching back to the Prophet. The member receives a wird, a set of daily recitations: phrases asking forgiveness, blessings on the Prophet, the words of Allah's oneness. The heart of it is dhikr, remembrance, and orders point to surah al-Ra'd, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Two orders by name. The Tijaniyyah honors Shaykh Ahmad al-Tijani and is spread across West and North Africa and beyond. Its members keep a daily wird and gather for group remembrance, and some travel to visit their founder's resting place in Fez. The Muridiyyah grew in Senegal around Shaykh Ahmadu Bamba. Murids are known for teaching that honest work, offered to God, is part of worship, and for the holy city of Touba, where the order's life gathers. In Indonesia, Turkey and South Asia, orders such as the Naqshbandiyya and the Qadiriyya keep their own circles. Last, the debate, told fairly. Some Muslims, including Salafis, criticize practices they see around some orders, such as visiting shrines or giving a shaykh great authority. Sufis answer that their remembrance, their love for the Prophet and their discipline all come from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and that a teacher is a guide, not a substitute for Allah. The conversation continues, inside the orders and outside them.
screen: `A TARIQA: A PATH WITH A GUIDE.` · `THE WIRD AND THE HEART AT REST.` · `TIJANIYYAH AND MURIDIYYAH.` · `THE DEBATE, TOLD FAIRLY.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be slow and even, like the circle in the courtyard. If you pray, quietly repeat subhan Allah, glory be to Allah, once on each out-breath; if you don't, simply count the breaths and notice how a repeated thing slowly quiets the mind.
Traditional Sufi orders today. Living paths of remembrance, each with a teacher, a daily wird and a community, from Senegal to Indonesia. Today's word.
Your line: the orders today. A circle before dawn, and then off to work. Next, Shia communities today.

1374.title: Shia communities today
1374.hook: in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond
1374.howItsDone: Shia Muslims pray toward the Ka'bah like other Muslims, often joining the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, and placing the forehead on a small clay tablet; they gather in mosques and in halls called husayniyyas or imambargahs, and Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orders today: a tariqa, a shaykh, a daily wird, and hearts at rest in remembrance.

A small disc of baked clay, about the size of a coin, sits on a prayer mat. When the person praying bows down, the forehead touches the clay. You'll find discs like that in homes in Baghdad and Beirut, Baku and Manama, Karachi and Lucknow, Detroit and London. It's one quiet sign of a Shia household, among others. The communities around it speak Arabic, Persian, Azerbaijani, Urdu, English. They live in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond. What holds them together?
screen: `A DISC OF CLAY ON THE MAT.` → `BAGHDAD, BAKU, KARACHI, DETROIT.` → `WHAT HOLDS THEM TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: Shia is short for shi'at Ali, a phrase Shia Muslims explain as the followers of Ali. Shia Muslims hold that after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, leadership belonged to his household, beginning with Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and passing through a line of Imams. They point, among other texts, to a hadith that Sunni collections keep too. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people: the Book of Allah, and his household, whom he asks them to remember. There are branches. The Twelvers, named for the line of Imams they recognize, are one. Zaydis, found especially in Yemen, and Isma'ilis, tomorrow's lesson, are others with their own histories. Then the places that hold a community. In Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain there is the husayniyya, a hall for gathering and mourning Husayn; in Pakistan and India the same kind of hall is called an imambargah. There are seminaries in Najaf and Qom, where students train for years. And Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law, so a believer in Chicago may follow a scholar in Najaf. Last, the shared floor. Shia and Sunni Muslims pray toward the same Ka'bah, fast the same Ramadan, go on the same Hajj and read the same Qur'an. Shia often join the noon prayer with the afternoon, and the sunset prayer with the night, and pray on that clay disc, which they explain as bowing onto earth, not onto a carpet. Different customs, the same direction.
screen: `SHI'AT ALI: THE FOLLOWERS OF ALI.` · `TWELVERS, ZAYDIS, ISMA'ILIS.` · `HUSAYNIYYA, IMAMBARGAH, SEMINARY.` · `THE SAME KA'BAH, THE SAME QUR'AN.`

1375.title: The Isma'ilis
1375.hook: a Shia community led today by a living Imam, the Aga Khan, known for development work
1375.howItsDone: Isma'ili Muslims recognize a living Imam, the Aga Khan, as the guide of their time; they gather for prayer in a jamatkhana, and the community supports the Aga Khan Development Network's schools, hospitals and rural programs with volunteered time and giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shia communities today: the followers of Ali, from Baghdad to Lucknow, praying toward the same Ka'bah.

What happens when a question comes up that nobody in the first centuries ever faced? A new medicine. A new kind of work. A family that has moved to a country with different laws. Muslim communities have their own ways of answering. Some open the books of the schools. Some ask a mufti. Some ask a marja'. One community turns to a living Imam, a descendant of the Prophet's family, whom they recognize as the guide for their own time. His title is the Aga Khan. The community is the Isma'ilis.
screen: `A QUESTION NOBODY FACED BEFORE.` → `BOOKS, MUFTI, MARJA'.` → `A LIVING IMAM.`

segments.voice: Isma'ilis are Shia Muslims who trace their line of Imams through Isma'il, a son of the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and they take their name from him. Twelver Shia followed a different son, which is where the two branches part. The Isma'ilis described here hold that the line of Imams has never been broken, and that there is always a present Imam, the Imam of the time. They point to a verse in surah al-Nisa, in Pickthall's words: "Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority". For them, those in authority include the Imam. Sunni scholars read the same words differently, as rulers or people of knowledge. Each reads it within its own tradition. Isma'ilis gather in a jamatkhana, a house for the community's prayer and meeting. In South Asian communities, devotional songs called ginans are part of that life. Isma'ilis speak of the outward form of faith and its inward meaning, and see the Imam as a guide to both. Then the work. The Imam has built institutions grouped as the Aga Khan Development Network: schools, hospitals, rural support, care for historic buildings, help in places of poverty, open to people of every faith. Isma'ilis explain this as faith that cares for life in this world as well as the next. Volunteering, giving time and skill, is woven through the community's life.

1376.title: Converts and reverts
1376.hook: people who come to Islam, called reverts by some, who often face welcome and challenges
1376.howItsDone: A person becomes Muslim by bearing witness, the shahada, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger; some mosques welcome new Muslims with study circles, mentors and invitations to iftar, and some communities ask which word, convert or revert, a person prefers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Isma'ilis: a living Imam, the jamatkhana, and work open to everyone.

Her first Ramadan, she breaks the fast alone at her kitchen counter with a date and a glass of water, because her family doesn't fast and she doesn't know anyone at the mosque yet. Her second Ramadan, somebody she met at Friday prayer texts her an address and the words: come, we'll save you a seat. Same woman, same faith, same dates on the plate. What changed was one text message. Some people who come to Islam as adults tell stories like hers. Some call themselves converts. Some call themselves reverts.
screen: `A DATE, ALONE AT THE COUNTER.` → `WE'LL SAVE YOU A SEAT.` → `CONVERT OR REVERT?`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred fifty-one, i said everyone started new. Today, a closer look. Some new Muslims prefer revert, and explain it from a hadith in al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: every child is born upon the fitra, the natural disposition, and it is the parents who shape the child into one way or another. If every person begins on that disposition, coming to Islam is a return, not a switch. Others are happy with convert, or new Muslim. The kindest move: ask which word they use. The door is a sentence. A person becomes Muslim by bearing witness, the shahada: there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. No class must be finished first. And the Qur'an insists the choice is free, in Pickthall's words: "There is no compulsion in religion." Nobody here starts as an insider. In the first generation, no one had been raised Muslim. Khadijah. Abu Bakr. Bilal, who had been enslaved. Tradition tells of Salman the Persian, who searched through teacher after teacher and land after land before reaching Madinah. Welcome and challenge are both real. Surah al-Tawbah names among those who may receive zakat the ones whose hearts are to be brought close, and scholars have included new Muslims among them. Some mosques run circles for new Muslims and invite them to iftars. And new Muslims describe the hard parts: a family that doesn't understand, learning the prayers in Arabic, not knowing which customs are faith and which are culture, and the loneliness of an Eid with nowhere to go.
screen: `REVERT: A RETURN TO THE FITRA.` · `THE DOOR IS A SENTENCE.` · `THE COMPANIONS WERE NEWCOMERS.` · `WELCOME AND CHALLENGE, BOTH REAL.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you were the new one, at a school, a job, a city, a dinner where you knew nobody, and the person who made it a little easier. What did they actually do: remember your name, save you a seat, ask you a question? Hold that small act for a few breaths, and if you pray, thank Allah for that person in your own words.
Converts and reverts. People who come to Islam as adults; some say revert, as a return to the fitra, some say convert. Ask which word they use. Today's word.
Your line: new to it. A saved seat can change a whole Ramadan. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1377.title: Muslim women's voices
1377.hook: Muslim women speak for themselves on dress, work, scholarship and faith, and they don't all agree
1377.howItsDone: Muslim women teach in mosques and schools, narrate and study hadith, write and speak on law and faith, and lead women's study circles; they hold a range of views on dress, work and mosque space, and argue for them in their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, converts and reverts: a return to the fitra, a door that's a sentence, and a seat saved.

A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint about her husband. He has spoken an old pagan formula over her, and by the custom of the time it means she is cut off from him, neither married nor free. She argues her case. She doesn't let it drop. She turns her complaint to Allah. And the surah that opens with her story is named for her argument: al-Mujadila, she who disputes. Its first verse says that Allah has heard the woman who pleaded with the Prophet about her husband. Her name, tradition says, was Khawlah.
screen: `SHE ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AL-MUJADILA: SHE WHO DISPUTES.` → `ALLAH HAS HEARD HER.`

segments.voice: Khawlah wasn't alone. Tradition says Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife, asked why the Qur'an spoke of men and not of women, and that a verse in surah al-Ahzab came down naming both, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe". And 'A'ishah became a teacher whom companions consulted. In Sahih Muslim, she praises the women of the Ansar, saying, in paraphrase, that shyness didn't keep them from learning their religion. Tradition also remembers women who narrated hadith and taught it, with men among their students, and that line of women teaching continues in schools and mosques today. Today's voices come in the plural. Muslim women write on law, run clinics, lead businesses, raise families, recite the Qur'an, preach to women's gatherings, and argue in public, on dress, work, mosque space and scholarship. And they don't all agree. Some argue from the classical schools. Some propose fresh readings of the texts. Some wear hijab and some don't, and both explain their reasons. Some work outside the home and some choose not to, and give their reasons too. These disagreements happen among Muslim women themselves; nobody needs an outsider, or a narrator, to settle them. What a listener can do is notice who is speaking. A Muslim woman, in her own words? Or someone speaking about her?

1378.title: Hijab, many choices
1378.hook: the hijab worn as devotion, with views and practices that vary
1378.howItsDone: Muslim women who wear hijab cover their hair in front of men outside their close family, in styles that vary by region and taste; classical scholars teach it as required, some contemporary writers read the verses as a call to modesty, and women's own practice and reasons vary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslim women's voices: from Khawlah to today, speaking for themselves, and not always agreeing.

A pin between the teeth. A mirror by the door. A length of soft fabric wrapped once, tucked, pinned, checked. The woman doing it is also finding her keys and telling her son to put his shoes on. To a stranger it might look like a statement. To her it's part of leaving the house. Maybe her grandmother wore one; maybe she never did. Either way, this woman decided for herself. Her sister, beside her, doesn't wear one at all. Same family, same faith, same mirror. And in the Qur'an, the word for that fabric means something else.

segments.voice: Day one hundred thirty-nine asked why hijab; today, the word and its readings. In the Qur'an, hijab doesn't name a headscarf. It means a screen or a curtain. In surah al-Ahzab, people who need to ask the Prophet's wives for something are told, in paraphrase, to ask from behind a curtain, and that curtain is a hijab. Then the verses about dress. In surah al-Nur, believing men are told first to lower their gaze and guard their modesty. Then believing women are told the same, and to draw their khimar, their head-covering, over their chests. Another verse in al-Ahzab speaks of women drawing their outer garments around them so they may be recognized and not troubled. The headscarf people call hijab today comes from how these verses have been read. Scholars of the classical schools, Sunni and Shia, read them as requiring a woman to cover her hair in front of men outside her close family. Some contemporary Muslim writers read them as a call to modesty that each woman shapes for herself. Muslim women hold both views, and speak for both. The practice varies too. Some wear it from childhood, some start as adults, some cover only for prayer, some wear it and later stop, some start again. Styles change from Jakarta to Cairo to Dearborn. And the reasons women who wear it give are their own: devotion to Allah, obedience, a reminder through the day, identity, privacy. Some who see it as required still describe it as something offered to Allah, a duty taken up with the heart.

1379.title: Young Muslims
1379.hook: youth groups, nasheed, online study circles
1379.howItsDone: Young Muslims gather in mosque youth groups and campus student associations for study circles, service projects and iftars, sing and share nasheed, and join online study circles that read the Qur'an and its commentaries together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hijab: in the Qur'an a curtain, today a head-covering, worn for reasons women give themselves.

A Thursday night video call. Small squares on a screen: a student in a dorm room with headphones on, a young nurse just off shift, someone in a parked car with the dome light on. One shares a page of tafsir, a commentary on the Qur'an, and they read it together, line by line, and argue gently about what it means. Somebody's little brother wanders into frame and waves. Nobody planned this in a mosque office. They planned it in a group chat.

segments.voice: The Qur'an has its own pictures of the young, starting in a cave. Surah al-Kahf tells of the people of the cave, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance." Young people, holding on in a city that didn't share their faith. Elsewhere, Ibrahim's people describe him as a youth, the young man who spoke against their idols. In al-Bukhari, among those the Prophet, peace be upon him, says Allah will shade on a day when there is no other shade, he names, in paraphrase, a young person who grew up in the worship of Allah. Growing up faithful is named on its own, in the same list as the just ruler. And now? Mosque youth groups and campus student associations run study circles, sports nights, food drives and late Ramadan iftars. Nasheed, songs of praise and devotion, are sung by young voices, some with only voice and drum, because some scholars discourage instruments, and some with instruments, because others permit them; day one hundred forty-eight looked at why scholars differ. Online study circles gather young people from different cities around a text. And the hard part, said plainly: some young Muslims carry questions about identity, about belonging, about the distance between their parents' customs and their own lives. They also carry the faith forward into new languages and new places. The people of the cave didn't wait to be old enough to matter, and neither does the Thursday night call.

segments.voice: Think of someone younger whose life you touch, a child, a niece, a student, a teenager down the street, and one thing they're trying to do: learn, build, believe, belong. For a few breaths, simply wish them well in it, and if you pray, ask Allah to increase them in guidance, in your own words.
